statements.label: supported
statements.text: In human breast cancer cells, knocking out MALAT1 made the cells more metastatic, and re-expressing Malat1 reversed this gain.
statements.evidence: Similarly, knockout of MALAT1 in human breast cancer cells induces their metastatic ability, which is reversed by re-expression of Malat1.
statements.note: The abstract reports that MALAT1 knockout induces metastatic ability in human breast cancer cells and that Malat1 re-expression reverses it.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The study found that higher MALAT1 levels accompany lower breast cancer progression and metastatic ability.
statements.evidence: Moreover, MALAT1 levels inversely correlate with breast cancer progression and metastatic ability.
statements.note: An inverse correlation means higher MALAT1 levels go with lower progression and metastatic ability, exactly as the abstract states.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Inactivating Malat1 in the transgenic mouse model of breast cancer accelerated the growth of the primary mammary tumours.
statements.evidence: We show here, however, that targeted inactivation of the Malat1 gene in a transgenic mouse model of breast cancer, without altering the expression of its adjacent genes, promotes lung metastasis, and that this phenotype can be reversed by genetic add-back of Malat1.
statements.note: The abstract reports only that Malat1 inactivation promotes lung metastasis and says nothing, either way, about primary tumour growth.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: By binding TEAD, the MALAT1 lncRNA inactivates this prometastatic transcription factor and keeps it from engaging YAP and its target gene promoters.
statements.evidence: Mechanistically, the MALAT1 lncRNA binds and inactivates the prometastatic transcription factor TEAD, preventing TEAD from associating with its co-activator YAP and target gene promoters.
statements.note: The abstract states that MALAT1 binds and inactivates TEAD, preventing its association with the co-activator YAP and with target gene promoters.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: High FTO levels in human melanoma predict shorter patient survival.
statements.evidence: FTO level is increased in human melanoma and enhances melanoma tumorigenesis in mice.
statements.note: The abstract reports raised FTO in human melanoma and tumorigenesis effects in mice but gives no data linking FTO levels to patient survival.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Knocking down FTO raised m6A methylation on protumorigenic melanoma genes such as PD-1, CXCR4 and SOX10, which increased their RNA decay through the reader YTHDF2.
statements.evidence: Knockdown of FTO increases m 6 A methylation in the critical protumorigenic melanoma cell-intrinsic genes including PD-1 (PDCD1), CXCR4, and SOX10, leading to increased RNA decay through the m 6 A reader YTHDF2.
statements.note: The abstract states that FTO knockdown increases m6A on PD-1, CXCR4 and SOX10 and that this leads to increased RNA decay via YTHDF2.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In mice, lowering FTO made melanoma more sensitive to anti-PD-1 therapy, and this sensitization relied on adaptive immunity.
statements.evidence: Knockdown of FTO sensitizes melanoma cells to interferon gamma (IFNγ) and sensitizes melanoma to anti-PD-1 treatment in mice, depending on adaptive immunity.
statements.note: The abstract reports that FTO knockdown sensitizes melanoma to anti-PD-1 treatment in mice in a manner that depends on adaptive immunity.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Metabolic starvation stress triggers FTO induction, which proceeds through autophagy and the NF-κB pathway.
statements.evidence: FTO is induced by metabolic starvation stress through the autophagy and NF-κB pathway.
statements.note: The abstract states that metabolic starvation stress induces FTO via the autophagy and NF-κB pathway.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Caprin1 binding to G3BP promotes stress granule formation while USP10 binding suppresses it, and the two partners cannot bind G3BP at the same time.
statements.evidence: Caprin1/USP10 binding to G3BP is mutually exclusive: Caprin binding promotes, but USP10 binding inhibits, SG formation.
statements.note: The abstract states that Caprin1 and USP10 bind G3BP mutually exclusively, with Caprin promoting and USP10 inhibiting SG formation.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Re-expressing the G3BP1 F33W mutant, which cannot bind Caprin1 or USP10, rescued stress granule formation, but the phosphomimetic S149E mutant did not.
statements.evidence: Rescue experiments using G3BP1 mutants show that phosphomimetic G3BP1-S149E fails to rescue SG formation, whereas G3BP1-F33W, a mutant unable to bind G3BP partner proteins Caprin1 or USP10, rescues SG formation.
statements.note: The rescue experiments described show S149E failing and F33W, a Caprin1/USP10-binding-deficient mutant, succeeding in restoring SG formation.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Through its RGG motif G3BP associates with 40S ribosomal subunits, and the same motif is needed for G3BP to drive stress granule formation.
statements.evidence: G3BP interacts with 40S ribosomal subunits through its RGG motif, which is also required for G3BP-mediated SG formation.
statements.note: The abstract states that the RGG motif mediates G3BP binding to 40S subunits and is also required for G3BP-mediated SG formation.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Cells lacking both G3BP1 and G3BP2 survive stresses that trigger eIF2α phosphorylation less well than normal cells.
statements.evidence: We now show that cells lacking both G3BP1 and G3BP2 cannot form SGs in response to eukaryotic initiation factor 2α phosphorylation or eIF4A inhibition, but are still SG-competent when challenged with severe heat or osmotic stress.
statements.note: The abstract reports only whether the double-knockout cells form stress granules, not how well they survive any stress.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The dipeptide repeat proteins GR and PR insert into liquid assemblies of LCD-containing proteins, alter their phase separation and change their material properties.
statements.evidence: Furthermore, we show that GR and PR altered phase separation of LCD-containing proteins, insinuating into their liquid assemblies and changing their material properties, resulting in perturbed dynamics and/or functions of multiple membrane-less organelles.
statements.note: The abstract states that GR and PR alter phase separation of LCD-containing proteins by insinuating into their liquid assemblies and changing their material properties.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Lowering GR and PR levels in C9ORF72 mouse models prevented neurodegeneration.
statements.evidence: Genetic analysis in Drosophila demonstrated the functional relevance of these interactions to DPR toxicity.
statements.note: The only in vivo work the abstract mentions is genetic analysis in Drosophila; it reports no mouse experiments and no protection from lowering DPR levels.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: More than half of the proteins that interact with GR or PR are components of membrane-less organelles such as nucleoli, the nuclear pore complex and stress granules.
statements.evidence: Indeed, most GR/PR interactors are components of membrane-less organelles such as nucleoli, the nuclear pore complex and stress granules.
statements.note: The abstract states that most, i.e. a majority, of GR/PR interactors are components of membrane-less organelles such as these.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The arginine-containing dipeptide repeats GR and PR were found to bind RNA-binding proteins and proteins carrying low complexity sequence domains.
statements.evidence: find that arginine-containing DPRs, polyGly-Arg (GR) and polyPro-Arg (PR), interact with RNA-binding proteins and proteins with low complexity sequence domains (LCDs)
statements.note: The interactome analysis in the abstract found that GR and PR interact with RNA-binding proteins and LCD-containing proteins.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Dup15q, a genetically defined form of ASD caused by a chromosome 15q11.2-13.1 duplication, shows the same core transcriptomic signature as idiopathic ASD.
statements.evidence: We further demonstrate that a genetically defined subtype of ASD, chromosome 15q11.2-13.1 duplication syndrome (dup15q), shares the core transcriptomic signature observed in idiopathic ASD.
statements.note: The abstract states that dup15q shares the core transcriptomic signature seen in idiopathic ASD.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Across the first two decades of life, network analysis found altered age-related trajectories of microglial and synaptic function in individuals with ASD.
statements.evidence: Co-expression network analysis reveals that individuals with ASD show age-related changes in the trajectory of microglial and synaptic function over the first two decades
statements.note: The co-expression network analysis reported age-related changes in microglial and synaptic function trajectories in ASD over the first two decades.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: SOX5 expression is lower in the cortex of individuals with ASD than in controls.
statements.evidence: Our data suggest that SOX5, a transcription factor involved in neuron fate specification, contributes to this reduction in regional differences.
statements.note: The abstract links SOX5 to the reduced frontal-temporal differences but does not report whether, or in which direction, SOX5 expression changes in ASD.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In ASD, splicing of activity-dependent neuron-specific exons was reduced, and gene expression differences between frontal and temporal lobes were smaller than normal.
statements.evidence: downregulation of the alternative splicing of activity-dependent neuron-specific exons, and attenuation of normal differences in gene expression between the frontal and temporal lobes
statements.note: The abstract reports downregulated alternative splicing of these exons and attenuated normal frontal-temporal expression differences in ASD.
